source.title: Wukong: Towards a Scaling Law for Large-Scale Recommendation
source.authors: Bu-Yun Zhang; Liang Luo; Yu-Xin Chen; Jade Nie; Xi Liu; Daifeng Guo; Yanli Zhao; Shen Li; Yuchen Hao; Yan-Tao Yao; G. Lakshminarayanan; Ellie Wen; Jongsoo Park; M. Naumov; Wen-Lin Chen

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as motivation, but its experiments measure recommendation models and recommendation prediction loss, not held-out pretraining loss of language models or the claim’s other named outcomes.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling results concern Wukong and other recommendation architectures on an internal recommendation dataset. They do not test any listed version: recommendation log loss is not language-model pretraining loss, and recommendation is not one of the specified downstream-task or modality/training-regime tests. Public-dataset benchmark results and cited findings from other papers are not results on the claim.
record.test_reason: V5 asks whether the same power-law form holds outside text pretraining. The study fits a power law, y = −100 + 99.56x^0.00071, to recommendation-model log loss against compute (GFLOP/example). The fit spans two orders of magnitude on a 146B-example dataset. It also reports loss against parameter count and data volume. This is a new domain with a result on V5. No language-model results are reported, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Wukong establishes a scaling law for recommendation across two orders of magnitude of compute, beyond 100 GFLOP/example, where prior architectures plateau. They add that Wukong stays ahead of state-of-the-art baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use a stacked factorization-machine recommendation architecture and recommendation prediction metrics, not the language-model pretraining-loss setups in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that Wukong’s response to scaling individual components differs: increasing layer count and MLP size substantially improves quality, while nL plateaus for the base configuration (Section 7.3, Figure 5).

fits_no_version.finding: Larger Wukong models are more data-efficient, reaching the same quality improvement with fewer samples (Appendix E, Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation models, larger models need fewer examples to reach a given loss improvement.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling the number of layers and the MLP size improves Wukong loss substantially, while nL plateaus at the base config (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within Wukong, which hyperparameter is scaled affects the loss gain.

record.problems: The scaling evaluation is on one internal dataset; uncertainty estimates are not reported. The authors state that they have not reached the complexity level where Wukong’s scalability limit applies. The results concern recommendation loss, not the language-model claim.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many individual recommendation-model scaling configurations in Appendix C, Table 5, and benchmark results on six public datasets in Table 2. These do not test a listed claim version; the main Wukong scaling findings are captured in r1–r3.

untested.parts: Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Power-law fits for parameters and data separately, as opposed to compute.
All parts; no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All parts; no small-run fits are used to predict much larger runs.
All parts; no compute-optimal parameter/token split is measured.
All parts; the component scaling in Fig. 5 is not at a fixed parameter count.
All parts; no fitting-choice sensitivity is studied.

missing.what: Baseline models' loss vs compute scaling: plateaus for DLRM, FinalMLP and AFN+, and instability for DCNv2 and AutoInt+.
Wukong Task2 scaling values, which mirror Task1 (e.g. −0.32 to −0.76 relative LogLoss).
Loss vs training compute in PF-days for Wukong.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'discusses/T6' classification is overturned: recommendation is a non-text domain, and the paper fits a power law there, which is what V5 asks about. The exponent is tiny and is fitted on relative LogLoss, not absolute loss. The data are from one internal dataset with no uncertainty reported. The public-dataset AUC table compares methods and is rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out language-model pretraining loss are measured.
No small-run fits are evaluated against substantially larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute optimum over language-model parameter and token allocation is measured.
The study does not test how language-model architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count.
Recommendation experiments do not test the stated power-law claim for other modalities or training regimes.
Recommendation prediction quality is not downstream performance of language models or a test of its predictability from pretraining loss.
No fitting-choice sensitivity or disagreement among language-model scaling-law fits is tested.

rows.subject: Wukong
rows.size_stated: scaling sweep across two orders of magnitude in model complexity; beyond 100 GFLOP/example
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model compute complexity on the internal recommendation dataset.
rows.value: empirically, y = −100 + 99.56x^0.00071; approximately a 0.1% improvement for every quadrupling of complexity
rows.locator: Section 7.2, Quality vs. Compute Complexity; Figure 1
rows.note: This is recommendation prediction loss, not language-model pretraining loss.
rows.check: The record links this row to none, but it is a fitted power law of recommendation loss vs compute over ~0.5–108 GFLOP/example, which bears on V5. The baseline is a relative LogLoss reference (basic DLRM), not a control. No uncertainty is reported.

rows.subject: Wukong
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model parameter count on the internal recommendation dataset.
rows.value: steady improvement trend up to over 637 billion parameters
rows.locator: Section 7.2, Quality vs. Model Size; Figure 3
rows.note: The paper also says Wukong outperforms baselines by roughly 0.2% across model-size scales.
rows.check: The record links this row to none. Loss improves steadily with parameter count, but no power-law fit is given for parameters. The sparse embedding table is fixed at 627B, so only dense parameters (~0.7–17B) vary. The total of 637B+ overstates the scaled range.

rows.subject: Wukong
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated one-pass training on increasing amounts of training data.
rows.value: All Wukong models consistently improved in quality through the end of 146B data; larger models had a steeper quality-improvement trend and were more data-efficient.
rows.note: The prose describes the trends; no exact plotted values are stated.
rows.check: The record links this row to none. Training is one pass and quality keeps improving up to 146B examples, but no power-law fit for data is reported. The authors note the large models have not converged, and no baseline is stated.

relationships.condition: Wukong architecture, internal recommendation dataset, compute scaling (Task1; Task2 reported as comparable)
relationships.reason: r1: power-law fit of loss vs GFLOP/example holds over two orders of magnitude, roughly 0.1% gain per 4x compute; r2 and r3 show continued improvement with dense parameters and data.
relationships.display_finding: The compute power-law fit held across two orders of magnitude with roughly 0.1% gain per fourfold compute increase, alongside continued gains from dense parameters and data.

relationships.condition: Other recommendation architectures (DLRM, FinalMLP, AFN+, DCNv2, AutoInt+, MaskNet) on the same dataset
relationships.reason: Per the text and Table 5 (no row records this), the baselines plateau, e.g. DLRM beyond 31 GFLOP and FinalMLP beyond 36. AFN+ does not improve, and others hit loss explosion or OOM. So the scaling trend in recommendation depends on architecture.
relationships.display_finding: DLRM plateaued beyond 31 GFLOP and FinalMLP beyond 36 GFLOP, while AFN+ failed to improve and other baselines encountered exploding loss or memory exhaustion.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
